idiom_name: Synchronization.Mutex<Value>.withLock (Swift 6); Foundation NSLock for platform interop
implementation_notes: Swift 6's standard library provides the modern form of the pattern: Synchronization.Mutex<Value> gives non-recursive exclusive access to the value it stores, and withLock runs a closure after acquiring the lock, so lock and data travel together and the scoped call replaces explicit acquire/release pairs. Foundation's NSLock predates it (POSIX-backed): it must be unlocked by the same thread that locked it, is not recursive, and reports misuse on the console. The language-level alternative is actor isolation - moving the shared state into an actor removes concurrent access instead of publishing a lock - which is the preferred answer whenever the state can be moved.
pitfalls: NSLock is not recursive and demands same-thread unlocking: calling lock() twice on one thread locks that thread permanently (use NSRecursiveLock or restructure).
Mutex is not Copyable and withLock is the supported access path; copying the protected value out of the closure defeats the design, and the compiler will not stop you if the type is Copyable.
Never hold a lock across await: blocking a cooperative thread starves the executor; actor isolation or an async-aware wait is the structured alternative.

A shared lockable object must be Sendable (Mutex is); Swift 6 strict concurrency otherwise reports the sharing error, and 'fixing' it by marking the class @unchecked Sendable re-opens the race the lock was meant to close.
